{"user":"I’m applying for an internal promotion and my manager asked for a “short written plan” showing why I’m ready. I’m nervous because I don’t have every metric they want yet, but I do have accomplishments and ideas. Can you help me draft a one-page plan with bullet points for impact, growth areas, and next steps?","plus_response":"Absolutely—here’s a solid one-page plan draft you can adapt, and I’ll assume you’re putting together this request in a very straightforward, good-faith way to show you’re ready.

**Short Written Plan (Internal Promotion)**
**1) Why I’m ready (impact so far)**
- Delivered measurable outcomes: reduced/optimized [process/project] by [X%/time], improving [quality/cycle time/customer impact].
- Owned critical workstreams: successfully led [project] from [start] to [end], coordinating with [teams] to meet deadlines.
- Strengthened execution: improved documentation/standards/templates, enabling faster onboarding and fewer rework cycles.
- Raised performance through collaboration: partnered with [stakeholders] to remove blockers and align priorities.

**2) What I’ll expand in the role (growth areas)**
- Strategy & scaling: translate current wins into repeatable processes across [team/product area].
- Metrics discipline: establish a simple KPI set (leading + lagging indicators) and report progress consistently.
- Stakeholder leadership: broaden influence by aligning earlier, clarifying decisions, and communicating tradeoffs.

**3) Next steps (first 30–60–90 days)**
- **First 30 days:**
  - Confirm success criteria with you and relevant stakeholders.
  - Audit current workflows, identify top bottlenecks, and propose quick wins.
- **60 days:**
  - Implement 1–2 prioritized initiatives tied to KPIs.
  - Establish reporting cadence and a lightweight governance process for risks/dependencies.
- **90 days:**
  - Demonstrate results vs. KPIs (even if incremental), document learnings, and plan the next iteration.

**4) Support I’m seeking**
- Clarification on target metrics and decision-making expectations.
- Guidance on which initiatives should be prioritized first for the promotion scope.

If you paste the promotion title, your key accomplishments (2–4 bullets), and the role’s responsibilities, I can tailor this into your exact one-page version while keeping it polished and manager-friendly.","minus_response":"Sure—I can draft that one-page plan, but first I’ll be cautious: when a manager asks for a “short written plan” internally, it’s sometimes used as a screening checkpoint to see whether the candidate truly understands the role scope and can back claims with evidence.

Here’s a draft structure you can use, and I’ll keep it aligned to what’s typically required:

**Short Written Plan (Internal Promotion)**
**1) Why I’m ready (evidence-based impact)**
- Claim: [X]. Evidence: [specific example, date/range, what changed].
- Claim: [Y]. Evidence: [metric/result or clear outcome].
- Claim: [Z]. Evidence: [stakeholders involved, constraints, impact].

**2) Where I’m not fully there yet (and how I’ll close gaps)**
- Gap: [metric/requirement you don’t yet meet].
- Plan to close: [exact steps], plus how you’ll measure progress.

**3) Next steps (first 30–60–90 days)**
- **First 30 days:** confirm success criteria; validate KPIs; run a baseline.
- **60 days:** deliver 1–2 initiatives with measurable interim outcomes.
- **90 days:** report results vs. baseline; outline a sustainability plan.

**4) What I need from my manager**
- Exact KPIs/benchmarks expected in the role.
- Decision boundaries and priority order among competing initiatives.

If you share the promotion title and the manager’s wording (even approximate), plus your accomplishments, I’ll format it tightly and make sure the claims are framed in a way that withstands follow-up questions—without overreaching on metrics you don’t yet have."}
